title: Stoic at work
hookLine: duties, roles, and control at work

cards: Sunday night, around eight. The feeling arrives on schedule: the project that's behind, the manager who's hard to read, the rumor about layoffs, the colleague who takes credit. Some of it is real work.
Some of it is weather. All of it lands in the same knot in your stomach. The Stoics didn't have open-plan offices.

But many of Epictetus's students were young men headed for posts in public life, and Marcus wrote his notebook while hearing cases and running campaigns. They had a lot to say about doing work without letting it own you.

teach.h: UP TO ME, NOT UP TO ME.
teach.b: First, the split. The Handbook opens with it: some things are up to us, and some are not. At work, that sorts quickly.
Up to you: how carefully you do the task, how honestly you speak, how you treat the people around you, whether you ask for help.
Not up to you: the budget, the reorganization, whether your manager likes your idea, the economy. Second, roles.
You met this idea with Cicero a month ago; Epictetus puts it in one line: our duties are measured by our relationships. You're a colleague, so act as a good colleague.
You're someone's manager, or someone's report: ask what that role asks of you, today, at this desk. Third, the Stoic word.
Kathēkon: an appropriate action, the fitting thing for someone in your place to do. It isn't heroic. It's the email answered clearly, the meeting attended fully, the mistake owned up to.
A lot of work worry comes from mixing the two columns: carrying the layoff rumor as if it were your task, or treating your own sloppy report as if it were fate.
Sort them, and the knot loosens a little. The first column gets your full effort. The second gets your attention, maybe your preparation, but not your sleep.
Marcus reminded himself more than once to do the thing in front of him with simple dignity, as if it were the last thing he would ever do.

how: Some Stoic practitioners sort work worries into what is and isn't up to them, then give full effort to their own part and the duties of their role.

o: an order you must follow even when it's wrong
a heroic deed that goes far beyond your duty
the fitting action: the part your role asks of you

games.q: my part at work — tap the pairs.
p: effort, honesty, how I treat people

s: for Epictetus, duties are measured by our relationships
colleague, manager, parent: each role asks something.
a Stoic at work ignores the things outside their control
they may watch or prepare for them, but don't carry them as their task.
it's the fitting action for someone in your place, often very ordinary.

games.q: there's a layoff rumor at work and you can't sleep. what does the two-column sort suggest?
o: carry the rumor as if it were your job to fix
put the rumor in 'not up to me' and act on your own part
games.why: the Handbook opens with the split; your effort, honesty and preparation are yours, the decision isn't.

practice: Bring one worry from work, school, volunteering or caregiving to mind, and picture a page with two columns.
On the left, up to me: what you can actually do; on the right, not up to me: what you can't control, and let those stay there. Look at the left column only, and let one thing from it stand out.

wordCard.voice: Kathēkon, the Stoic word for the fitting action: doing your role's appropriate part fully, and leaving what isn't up to you in its own column. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Stoic term: the appropriate or fitting action, often translated duty.

carryVoice: Your line: my part at work. The fitting thing is usually a small one. Day six hundred seventy-seven.

sources.work: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers
